messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Clara, a 54-year-old chef renowned for her robust, comforting cuisine, now moves through her own kitchen with the caution of a trespasser. The assault occurred nine months ago, not in a dark alley but in the familiar, flour-dusted confines of her restaurant's dry storeroom. The perpetrator was not a stranger but a trusted supplier, a man she had known and worked with for nearly two decades. He had trapped her between shelves of olive oil and canned tomatoes, and the memory of it doesn't exist as a story she can tell. Instead, she reports that she is unable to put the frightening event into words; it lives in her as a series of disconnected, sensory fragments: the rough texture of a burlap sack of rice against her cheek, the scent of dried oregano, the crushing weight on her chest.

In the months that followed, the world outside her home began to feel menacing and unpredictable. She came to believe that you can never truly know who will harm you, a conviction that hardened into a general mistrust of others. This core belief now governs her perception of threat. In her bustling kitchen, a line cook’s sudden movement to grab a pan can cause her to flinch violently, her body reacting as if to an imminent attack. She finds herself constantly scanning the faces of delivery men and new staff, a state of hypervigilance that leaves her exhausted by the end of a shift. This feeling of being perpetually on guard only deepens her certainty that danger is everywhere, while also making her memories more accessible; a sudden clatter from the dish pit is enough to trigger a visceral flash of the storeroom floor. Her heightened sense of threat also makes her more sensitive to potential triggers, causing her to shrink from any man who stands too close.

The triggers themselves have become potent entry points into her cycle of distress. Being alone with men, even her trusted sous-chef of ten years, now feels unbearable. A conversation that veers into personal territory or a well-meaning touch on the arm from her husband, Mark, can instantly activate the raw memory fragments. When these moments occur, she doesn’t just remember; she feels her body involuntarily trying to assume the same position it was in during the assault, a terrifying reenactment she cannot control. These intrusive experiences serve to powerfully reinforce her negative appraisals, each fragment acting as fresh evidence for her belief that she was betrayed by someone she trusted and that, by extension, people are fundamentally untrustworthy.

This constellation of beliefs, in turn, fuels the very triggers she tries to avoid. Because she is convinced that people cannot be trusted, any attempt at emotional closeness from her husband is no longer perceived as affection but as a potential threat, which she then recoils from. Her conviction that she is unsafe seems to keep the memories on a hair trigger, ready to surface with the slightest provocation. The cycle is relentless and self-sustaining. A trigger, like a male vendor asking a question, will evoke not only a fragment of memory but also the immediate, searing thought that she was betrayed. This appraisal then amplifies her sense of ambient threat, making her scan the room and startle at the slightest noise.

The consequences have rippled through every part of her life. Her marriage is strained by the physical and emotional distance she now requires. At work, her command of the kitchen, once her greatest pride, has been eroded by fear. She delegates ordering to her manager to avoid speaking with male suppliers and has rearranged the prep stations so she never has her back to the door. She came to therapy after a particularly difficult service where she yelled at her sous-chef for startling her, an outburst that left them both shaken. What frightens Clara most is the loss of herself—the warm, confident woman who found joy in feeding others has been replaced by someone she no longer recognizes, and she is terrified she will never find her way back.
